name: Shia Islamism
summary: Shia Islamism is the implementation of Twelver Shia Islam in politics, wanting public life and law organised around an Islamic vision. It includes Khomeinism, which gives supreme authority to a qualified jurist, and Iraqi movements such as the Dawa Party, which taught rule of the people and, in part, rejects clerical rule. The branches share the aim of an Islamic order but split on clerical rule, democracy and relations with Iran.
scope: Shia Islamism as the defining sources use the label: Islamism rooted in Shia Islam, which the scholarship treats as more clerical than the Sunni kind (Valbjørn and Gunning, citing Roy and Louër; s4) and as shaped since 1979 by the Islamic Republic of Iran as a working model of an Islamic state (POMEPS, s6). The sources count as its branches the followers of velayat-e faqih (Khomeini and Iran’s state, Hizbullah), the Shirazi network, Iraq’s Hizb al-Dawa (the first Shia Islamist party, formed in Najaf in 1957 around Baqir al-Sadr; s2), SCIRI/ISCI and the Sadrists, and Shia Islamist groups in Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Afghanistan and Pakistan (s4). Its formative period is the 1950s–60s in Iraq, when Baqir al-Sadr (Usus al-Dawla al-Islamiyya) and Taqi al-Mudarrisi drew on Sunni Islamists such as al-Banna, Mawdudi and Qutb and disputed whether clerics or the people hold sovereignty in an Islamic state (s5). It excludes Sunni Islamism, Shia religious quietism and non-political Shia Islam, and Shia politics with no Islamist aim; Khomeini’s doctrine of rule by the jurist has its own profile (Khomeinism), though s4 and s6 treat it as one branch of Shia Islamism.

two central actors in the formative period of Shi‘i Islamism in Iraq: Muḥammad Bāqir al-Ṣadr (1935–80) and Muḥammad Taqī al-Mudarrisī (b. 1945) and their earliest political writings in which they set out their visions of an Islamic state. Both figures were among the first Shi‘i activists to engage theoretically with the nature of an Islamic state and established and headed the two of the most prominent Islamist movements stemming from Iraq. Bāqir al-Ṣadr was the chief ideologue of Ḥizb al-Da‘wa al-Islāmiyya (Party of the Islamic Call) which he founded with other activists in 1957/58. His Usus al-Dawla al-Islāmiyya (Principles of the Islamic State), written around the time when the party was founded, became its first programmatic text.

sources.title: Our Economics (Iqtisaduna), English translation
sources.author: Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr
sources.usedFor: Sadr's own account of economics: his critique of Marxism and capitalism, the three forms of ownership, land and labour, usury, social security and social balance.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: In Sadr's account land is by nature the Imam's (the state office's) property, and individuals hold only a right earned by labour; he does not call all wealth state property. "The land is by its nature the property of Imām and no individual possesses the right to its permanent ownership" (s7)

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: Sadr's Usus makes countering Western imperialism part of the Islamic state's jihad, which can include military confrontation. "can include military confrontation as part of its jihād" (s5)

ban-cartels.rationale: Sadr lists monopolisation among the activities the sharia bans; he does not name cartels. "such as usury and monopolisation etc." (s7)

ban-interest.rationale: Sadr's Iqtisaduna lists usury among the activities Islam bans outright and says Islam denies owners the right to grow wealth by it. "banned certain economic and social activities, which, in the opinion of Islam, stand in the way of materialising the ideals and values adopted by Islam, such as usury and monopolisation etc." (s7) / "It denied the owner the right to grow the wealth which he owned by means of usury" (s7)

civilizational-union.rationale: Sadr endorses a politically united umma and a worldwide Islamic state as an ideal, while accepting separate states on pragmatic grounds. "He endorses the Pan-Islamic utopian ideal of a politically united umma and the aim to establish an Islamic state stretching the entire globe." (s5)

class-struggle-history.rationale: Sadr's critique of historical materialism rejects class struggle as the necessary engine of development and calls the idea falsified. "the idea of the class struggle inspired by that inconsistency stood falsified" (s7) / "Marxism also believes that no development takes place except through class struggle, between the class supporting the development and the other which tries to oppose it. But we find that the Japanese society entirely favoured the movement for industrial and capitalistic development" (s7)

clerical-rule.rationale: Documented split: Mudarrisi gives the jurist absolute leadership, while Sadr's Usus gives clerics advisory and judicial roles with the people ruling by shura, and Dawa taught rule of the people. "The just jurisconsult is the leader" (s5) / "Shūrā is the legitimate mode of decision-making in an Islamic state in the absence of an infallible leader" (s5) / "al-Sadr advocated the concept of wilayet al-umma" (s2)

consent-of-governed.rationale: Documented split: Sadr bases decision-making on the government of the people, while Mudarrisi rejects even limited popular sovereignty. "Shūrā is the legitimate mode of decision-making in an Islamic state in the absence of an infallible leader" (s5) / "Unlike other Islamists, Taqī al-Mudarrisī rejects even a limited popular sovereignty within the confines of the sharī‘a" (s5)

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Sadr says Islam prohibits extravagance and squandering, which limits consumption and frees money for production. "Islam has prohibited extravagance and squandering." (s7) / "It makes ready a great deal of money for productive expenditure instead of consumptive expenditure in the fields of extravagance and squandering." (s7)

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Sadr makes the Islamic state responsible for the living standard of every individual and sets the head of state the aim of lifting the poor to a common comfortable standard. "Islam has prescribed to the State the duty of providing social security in respect of the standard of living for all the individuals of the Islamic society" (s7) / "the aim laid down for the Head of the State is the business of joining backward individuals with a higher standard of life in the direction which will make certain a general comfortable standard of life" (s7)

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Mudarrisi says sovereignty is God's alone; Sadr's Usus has the Imam as holder of divine sovereignty and later has the people rule by God's delegation. "absolute sovereignty belongs to God" (s5) / "the people to whom God has delegated his sovereignty as part of their human vicegerency" (s5)

equal-outcomes.rationale: Sadr wants a balanced standard of living, not equal incomes, and accepts differences of degree. "the social balance would be a balance of the standard of living and not in a balance of income among the individual members of the society" (s7) / "It does contain certain degrees of differences in standards but does not comprise of crying capitalist contradictory standards of living." (s7)

harm-principle.rationale: Sadr says there is no freedom for activities that run against the ideals of the sharia, not only those that harm others (he speaks of economic activity). "there can be no freedom for an individual in respect of such kinds of activities which according to the sacred laws" (s7)

homestead-ownership.rationale: Sadr sets out two juristic views and prefers the one in which working a dead land gives a right of use, not ownership. "there is another juristic view which is more in harmony with the legislative texts" (s7) / "Restoration of the land to cultivation vests in him the right of the usufruct of the land and to benefit from it" (s7)

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Sadr's theory of distribution ties gain to labour spent (direct or stored in tools) and rejects gain with no labour behind it, such as usury. "the expended labour which the theory regards as the sole basis for the acquiring of gain is not merely the direct labour but includes stored labour also" (s7) / "such an earning of his would constitute an earning gains without putting expended labour" (s7)

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Sadr argues against Marx that work is not the only basis of value and that profit can be explained without the worker's labour creating all value. "So when Marx regarded work as the only basis of the value, he could not explain the surplus value (the profit) except by cutting a part of the value created by the worker." (s7) / "in the light of another meter for the value like the psychological meter, it is possible for us to explain the surplus value without being obliged to regard it as a part of the value which the worker creates" (s7)

land-use-tenure.rationale: Sadr says an individual's right to land lasts only while he keeps it in use; if he neglects it till it is waste, the right ceases. "The individual cannot retain his right to it except by keeping it continuously alive and putting in the necessary labour and efforts to that end. However if he neglects it and avoids cultivating it till it becomes a waste land his right ceases." (s7)

laws-from-scripture.rationale: In Sadr's Usus the state's laws must be informed by and not contradict the sharia; Mudarrisi calls Islamic government a perpetual requirement. "are entitled to arrive at laws pertaining to the organisation of the state that are informed by the principles of the sharī‘a and cannot contradict them" (s5) / "Islamic government is a perpetual requirement" (s5)

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The first part of Iqtisaduna is a critique of historical materialism, arguing that the economic factor does not decide history. "This clearly proves that a thinker does not always get inspiration to an ideology from economic reality" (s7) / "neither the industrial revolution has been the main factor in the formulation of the new China and the change of its system of government" (s7)

morality-needs-religion.rationale: Sadr holds that Islam's ideological and spiritual framework gives the moral power that limits freedom, and blames capitalism's lack of such frameworks. "The ideological and spiritual frameworks in which Islam moulds the personality by affording an opportunity to lead life and make history on its basis, have immense moral power" (s7) / "was bereft of all the moral and spiritual frameworks and values" (s7)

more-religion-public.rationale: Sadr's first principle is that Islam gives a complete social order Muslims must establish; Dawa sought a full Islamic political, social and economic system. "a complete social order" (s5) / "wanted to delineate a complete Islamic political, social and economic system" (s2)

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Sadr presents the Islamic economy as a third system, neither Capitalist nor Socialist, nor a blend of them. "it is wrong to call the Islamic society a Capitalist one" (s7) / "It is also wrong to regard it (Islamic Society) as an admixture of this and that" (s7)

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Sadr makes helping the poor a binding religious and financial duty of the rich (general reciprocal responsibility). "Islam intervenes and makes financial duties, whereby it seeks to bring about the reciprocal responsibility, obligatory religious duties" (s7) / "money (wealth) is taken from the rich to fulfil the (need of) the poor" (s7)

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: Sadr allows opposing an un-Islamic state, even by violence, where success is likely; Mudarrisi's network took a more confrontational line. "that can include violence, would promise success" (s5) / "espousing a more confrontational outlook towards the state" (s5)

priority-to-poor.rationale: Sadr gives the state the task of raising the living standard of the poor and has wealth taken from the rich for them. "the aim laid down for the Head of the State is the business of joining backward individuals with a higher standard of life" (s7) / "money (wealth) is taken from the rich to fulfil the (need of) the poor" (s7)

profit-exploitation.rationale: Sadr rejects the Marxist theory of surplus value: profit need not be value stolen from the worker. "that the owner should steal away from the worker some of the value created by the latter, so that the class struggle between the owner and the worker be an inevitable phenomenon under this system" (s7) / "this so-called theoretical inconsistency also vanished and the idea of the class struggle inspired by that inconsistency stood falsified" (s7)

property-fundamental.rationale: Sadr says Islam does not take private ownership as the general principle and lets the ruler restrict individuals' economic freedom. "it does not recognise private ownership as a general principle" (s7) / "restricting the freedom of the individuals in their activities" (s7)

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Sadr limits owners' authority where it harms society and has the ruler seize land left idle, though he grounds ownership in labour rather than in the common good. "it is natural, on this basis, to limit an owner’s authority over the free use of his property in a way which may cause injury to others and be detrimental to the interest of the society" (s7) / "Islam’s prescript ordaining seizure of land from the possession of its owner if he lets it remain idle or neglects it" (s7)

public-ownership.rationale: Sadr's Islamic economy has public and state ownership alongside private ownership and says restrictions on usury and hoarding leave big projects to public properties. "it adopts the principle of general (public) ownership as well as State ownership in respect of some kinds of wealth and capitals" (s7) / "leave, naturally, the working of big projects to public properties" (s7)

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Sadr separates unchangeable sharia rulings from laws that answer the needs of the time and shows concern for legal flexibility. "Bāqir al-Ṣadr is equally concerned about legal flexibility in socio-political matters" (s5)

religion-illusion.rationale: Sadr rebuts the Marxist account of religion as consolation of the oppressed, arguing religious belief does not reflect economic misery. "so it is not possible to give a class explanation of history or to regard it as an intellectual expression of the reflexion of the conditions of down-troddnness which surrounds the exploited class" (s7) / "it was not a reflection of their economic circumstances" (s7)

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: In Sadr's Usus the government chooses one fatwa among rival marja's and enforces it as state law. "If several marāji‘ co-exist and issue different fatwa s on a certain question, the government chooses one fatwa and implements as part of the state's laws or policies." (s5)

religious-nation.rationale: Sadr defines the Islamic state as an ideological state whose identity rests on shared adherence to Islam, not ethnic or territorial ties. "whose identity is based on a shared adherence to Islam rather than ethno-national ties or geographical boundaries" (s5)

self-interest-moral.rationale: Sadr faults capitalism for leaving behaviour to personal interest without a moral and spiritual framework, which he says led to oppression and greed. "the Capitalist method which provides freedom to every individual and enables him assess his attitude in the light of his personal interests which ultimately meet with public interests" (s7) / "colossal vacuum caused by the dispensing with the spiritual and moral entity of the society as the result of which the society was pervaded by different kinds of oppression, recklessness and greed" (s7)

separate-church-state.rationale: Sadr holds that Islam is a complete social order, and Mudarrisi calls limiting the jurist's authority to religion a Western ploy. "arguing that the secularisation of his authority is a Western ploy, implemented to weaken Islam" (s5) / "a complete social order" (s5)

separated-powers.rationale: Documented split: Sadr keeps judicial authority outside the government apparatus, while Mudarrisi's jurist combines executive, legislative and judicial power. "Judicial authority is germane to the clerics, must remain outside of state control" (s5) / "combining the executive, legislative and judicial authority of the state" (s5)

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Sadr lets the ruler prohibit or order activities to suit the Islamic ideals of society, and Mudarrisi makes Islamic morality depend on the state. "He can thus prohibit or order such activities as to suit the Islamic ideals of the society." (s7) / "seeks to make Islamic morality and its sustenance dependent on the state" (s5)

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Sadr keeps clerical judicial and legal authority outside state control; Mudarrisi puts the state under the jurist. "Judicial authority is germane to the clerics, must remain outside of state control" (s5) / "the state needs to respect and protect the legal and judicial autonomy of the ‘ulamā’" (s5)

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Sadr has zakat and khums taken from the rich for the poor; he gives no rates, so this is a mild yes. "this method may sometimes simply mean use of force to wrench tax from the rich to meet the needs of the poor" (s7) / "Imposition of continuously recovering permanent taxes to expend them as regards the purpose of social balance" (s7)

work-for-welfare.rationale: Sadr says Islam makes social security unlawful for able-bodied men who can work and bars them from living on alms. "Islam has declared as unlawful giving social security to able bodied men, who are capable of engaging themselves in economic activities, and has prevented them from living on alms." (s7)
